utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. The interpreters are ready to go? Good morning to you as well. So now we are awaiting the witness. (Pause)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, witness E.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You can hear me? Fine. Yesterday you made a solemn declaration which of course still applies today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you again for being here and this morning you are going to be answering the questions which Mr. Mikulicic is going to be putting to you, so counsel, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you your Honours and good morning. Good morning, witness E. My name is Goran Mikulicic I am Defence counsel for the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski, and I will ask you several questions now, and please do answer them to the best of your recollections. Your Honours, respecting the wish of the witness for protection, I would suggest that this part of the session be closed because I will ask him several questions which might relieve certain names publicly, so in accordance with the witness's wishes, I would kindly ask you to move into closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? Can you go along with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honours. I think private session, there is a difference between private session and closed session. I think private session achieves the same objective, it is just the sound not going outside, but certainly no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Now we are going to move into a private session, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My colleagues, do you have any questions for the witness? No. Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you please pull down the blinds? Witness E, you have now completed your testimony here. We do not have any further questions for you. The International Criminal Tribunal is thankful for your coming to testify here at The Hague. You can now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann and Mr. Mikulicic, maybe we could have a recess now, a fifteen-minute recess because I was told that it would be convenient to have two small breaks. We could perhaps come back at five minutes past ten, and then we will work until twenty minutes past eleven, and in order to make the best use of the time we have for the next witness. I think that is a good idea. Do you have any suggestions in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, that is fine, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence agrees as well, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, recess fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think now we are going to have an open hearing, so with regard to the further proceedings, I would like to consult the interpreters. I have indicated to you that we are going to go on until 11.20. Then we will have a break until 11.45, and then we are going to go from 11.45 until the end of our working today, that is to say, 1.15. I trust that is all suitable to everyone. No problems? Wonderful. Well, maybe you could show in the next witness, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I call Professor Stefano Bianchini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. Please read out the Solemn Declaration that the usher has just handed you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated, sir. You did not experience the events first-hand but, in legal terms, you are a witness here. Thank you very much for being here this morning, and I trust you are comfortable, that you are well-seated there, and you are now going to answer the questions from the counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Niemann. Please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Would you state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Stefano Bianchini,.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at this document that I now show you, and could you look through this document and tell me whether it is an accurate record of your curriculum vitae? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I can speak French/English, so I do not need this. I do not think I need it because it is -- yes, I know this. This is my curriculum vitae. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honours. Professor, do you teach East European History and Institutions at the Department of Political Science, University of Bologna, Programme of International Relations in Forli?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And are you the Director of the Post-graduate International Summer School on 'Post-Communist Transition and European Integration Processes', which has been established in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And are you the Director of the Centre of East European and Balkan Studies of the University of the city of Bologna and the central coordinator of the Europe and the Balkan International network?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you the Italian co-ordinator as a partner of the University of Amsterdam and the University of the Sorbonne in Paris and the University of Sofia of a Tempus-Phare Project for Bulgaria on Interethnic Relations, "Bugamin", and with the Sussex Institute of a new Tempus Project which involves the four Balkan Universities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you the Editor-in-Chief of a Series of Monographs on the "Europe and Balkan International Network"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And a Member of the Editorial Board of the Quarterly "Nationalities Papers" of the Association for the Studies of Nationalities as well as the Italian Review of Geo-politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you published several books and articles in different languages on Balkan studies, and Balkan issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Including contemporary history, political and economic questions related to the modernisation and political culture to the national question, and to the Balkan Italian relations since the beginning of the century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you speak fluently Serbo-Croat, and have you a knowledge adequate for most needs of English, and French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you also have some knowledge of the Russian and Spanish languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a result of you being able to speak Serbo-Croat and -- has Yugoslavia been a central focus of your studies since 1972?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And do you have many sources within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does your knowledge of the local language present you with opportunities to read on a continuous, or steady basis, newspapers, documents, and books in relation to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did you have an opportunity to work for a considerable time in the archives of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The SKY and Tito cabinet on different subjects related to the period between 1952 and 1961?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did you also meet numerous Yugoslavian policy-makers, journalists, and ordinary men and women of that country, and during those years did you have discussions with them in relation to the affairs of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And have you collected documentation, and had an opportunity to establish associations with numerous organisations in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, what was the political composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federation of Yugoslavia, prior to 1991 was set up by six republics and two autonomous regions. The republics were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia. The two autonomous regions of Kosovo and Vojvodina were included in the framework of the Serb Republic. This Federation ideal was originally federation close to communism. Communism was its ideology, while this ideology was a little bit different from that in the Soviet Union or from the so-called socialist block, since 1948. It was based on self-management, on a radical, gradually-developed, but radical devolution of the administration, on a lack of economic planning, on certain freedom of movement within and outside the country, but in any case, in a framework which was resistant to political democracy. I would like to stress here that even in the constitution self-management, in the fourth basic principle, in the constitution, the fourth basic principle, I mean the Constitution of 1974, the last one, man agement was considered a peculiar form of proletarian dictatorship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I wanted to ask you some questions about the ethnic composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in connection with that, would you please look at the document that I now show you, and by reference to this document, would you be so kind as to explain the ethnic composition of the SFRY in relation to the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There should be copies there for your Honours and each time, would you just show the document to Mr. Mikulicic? He has a copy of it, but so that he knows for sure the document that we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would ask you to place this on the ELMO screen beside you, and if you have occasion to want to point to any particular part of any of the documents that you are shown, would you please do so on the document on the screen there, rather than on the television screen because it will not work on a television screen. You have to also, unfortunately, point to something and then turn your head towards the microphone because your voice needs to be picked up in the translation booths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So managing that somewhat gymnastic exercise, would you mind now explaining to us the ethnic composition of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a table which was prepared here under my direction and knowledge. It has as as its source "Skipredleg" which is a Yugoslavian journal published in Belgrade. I had the opportunity to make a comparison with other sources, particularly in Croat Zagreb, and I think that on these numbers and percentages, there is no discussion within the former Yugoslav Republics. This is just a comparison between 1981, 1991. You can see that the main ethnic group was the Serb with a percentage around the 36 per cent, a little bit reduced in 1991. Then the Croats, more or less the same percentage, the same exactly. The Muslims, who are the third percentage with the 10 per cent in 1991. Then the Albanians, particularly concentrated in Kosovo, 9.3 per cent, then the Slovenes, 7.5 per cent, in 1991 and the Macedonians, 5.8 per cent. In this table I wanted to include the Yugoslavs. In this order you can see that Yugoslavs were 5.4 per cent in 1981, and 3 per cent in 1991. This is not exactly included in the, "Statistici Godinjak", that is the annual review of the figures on Yugoslavia published during the socialist period, because Yugoslav was included only in the end of the list as a group apart, not exactly considered as an ethnic group. They were considered more or less as those who gave an unknown nationality, or not well-defined nationalities. Generally, even in the former Yugoslavia, Yugoslavs, within the list of the ethnic groups were not considered an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, just, perhaps stopping there for a moment, there are two features of this chart that I would like to ask you about. Firstly, why the dates 1981 and 1991? Why have those two dates been selected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why I choose these? Because they are the most recent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And were they the dates that a census was carried out in the former Yugoslavia, 1981 and 1991? Are these the dates when the census was carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could be a census, just to understand the recent evolution of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say, sorry, that more or less in 1981 and 1991 the same questions were addressed, more or less in this topic to the ethnic composition of the Yugoslavia to the population, while previously in 1948 and 1961. For instance, they questioned particularly for Muslims, so this is the reason why I choose the last two census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, is there any particular explanation that you may have as to why the percentage of Yugoslavs drops, in fact, from 1981 to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many reasons. The most common reason in all former Yugoslavia was the impact, the disappointment in the longer term economic crisis, the crisis of communism. The League of Communists collapsed in January 1990, that is one year and some months before the census was done and the pressures of nationalistic waves in the country created a kind of disappointment towards the Yugoslav idea and this was one of the reasons for the diminishing percentage, or, the result of the pressures from the nationalist group which made a psychological pressure on the population to choose their ethnic groups. Let me add also that, for instance, in 1981 the main intellectuals attacked strongly when the result of the census was published. Those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, because they accused these people to have abandoned, renounced, their origin nationalities. Another question is that during the 1980s, often Yugoslavs were considered, particularly in the last years of this decade, as Serbs. If it is true --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that in 1981 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1991. The articles were published particularly in Zagreb but not only in Zagreb, by a colleague of mine between 1981, 1982 as a reaction to these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I just need to stop you. There is some confusion. Just confirm for us. Are you saying that this reaction was in 1981 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reactions against the Yugoslavs, this intellectual reactions was after the census of 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1981, so the first census, and one of the reasons, in addition, that was considered, during the 1980s, was that Yugoslavs were more or less Serbs, but if you see, if you make a comparison with 1991, you see that this diminishing percentage and absolute vote of the Yugoslavs did not increase the number significantly, the numbers of the Serbs. This means that probably they were shared more or less by all the groups, and it seems to me, particularly by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, I tender that, your Honours, that exhibit as the next exhibit in order. I think it is number 37. I would like to now take you to Bosnia Herzegovina itself in relation to the same question and show you a document which I would ask you to look at when giving an explanation of the ethnic break-up of that republic. Perhaps that could be given the next Prosecution number in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Professor, looking at this particular exhibit, can you give us an explanation of the distribution in terms of numbers of the ethnic population in Bosnia Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The sources are the same as the previous one, and this is the detail of the ethnic composition of Bosnia Herzegovina on the basis of the census in 1981 and 1991. I just mentioned the three main ethnic groups, the Muslims, the Serbs and the Croats, plus the Yugoslavs, because Yugoslavs had a particular role in Bosnia Herzegovina before the multi-party elections in 1990. They had even one representative in the Presidency of the Republic. So the Yugoslavs had a particular role, and this is the reason why. Then the others, which means a lot of small ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I tender that, your Honours, as the next exhibit. I would like you to look, in terms of the geographical distribution of the ethnic groups, at the map that I now show you, and could you explain the geographical distribution of the ethnic groups, having regard to this map that is now shown to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the map of Bosnia Herzegovina with -- you can see -- divided in municipalities. These are the main municipalities of Bosnia Herzegovina, on the basis of the census 1991. You can see for the Muslims has been chosen the green colour, for the Croats the red one, and for the Serbs the blue one. The map was available here in The Hague. I made the comparison with other sources I had, particularly with, "Natlas", published in Zagreb in 1983, and there are no significant disputes on this. You can see this is a map, a good map, because it allows you to see where an ethnic group had a specific majority over 50 per cent, and when this group had a relative majority in the areas. But what is important also to take into account, that for instance, because of the demographic balance, the concentration, for instance, of the Croats in the red area, you can see along the borders of Dalmatia, Croatia, south of Croatia, leave no -- but the name has been changed in Tomislavgrad or Alejgrude, Chaplijna, Prozo, and so on, this area had a minority group of Croats in comparison with all the Croats in Bosnia Herzegovina because they were concentrated mainly in Sarajevo in the centre and also in other areas. So you can see this area because it is not so populated with a so strong percentage of Croats, but the majority of the Croats living in Bosnia Herzegovina, by demographic point of view, were not in this area but in other areas of Bosnia, so this is just to give you an idea of the distribution of the population, but it is quite difficult to give you an exact picture of the distribution of the ethnic groups in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours, as the next exhibit in order. Professor, when was the Bosnian Muslim community first recognised, or established, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a complicated question, because the Muslim ethnic group has been contested both by the Croat and Serb side, both claimed that they were Croats or Serbs of Islamic religion. However, during the Second World War in a document -- this is very interesting -- in a document of the parties and organisations, "Slavnoc", which means the territorial organisation of the liberation movement in Bosnia Herzegovina, this document has been held two days before the Jijica conference and the Jijica conference was the conference when the Federation of Yugoslavia was established by the parties and movements led by Tito. So two days before this meeting, in a document of the Slavnoc, the Muslims are quoted as an ethnic group with the Serbs and the Croats of Bosnia. This quotation was not included two days after in the official documentation of "Afnoj", the second session. So they were recognised in a way in the Bosnian context, not in the Yugoslav context. So, Bosnia was in the least of the six future republics of Yugoslavia but not Muslim was titular nation of Bosnia in the Yugoslav context. So this created the situation that for instance in of 1948 the population had the opportunity to declare themselves as Croat Muslim, Serb Muslim or even Macedonian Muslim. You have to take into account that the Muslims are not concentrated only in Bosnia but even in the area between the Montenegro and Serbia, this is Sanjac and in other areas, minority Macedonia. For this reason, Macedonian Muslim. Then in 1961 the question was changed. There existed, the possibility, for the Muslims to declare themselves as Muslim or as an ethnic group, not as a nation but as an ethnic group, with this qualification. Then in 1971 as a nation, a titular nation, of Bosnia Herzegovina. So even during communism we had a gradual process in accepting the term of, "Muslim". Even the term, "Muslim", has been disputed, and now, those who are considered Muslims generally call themselves Bosniaks, not Bosnians because Bosnians are all the people living in Bosnia, Yugoslav, Serbs, Croats, Jews and so on and Muslims so Bosniaks means those who are not Serbs and Croats and Jews and the others, so the Muslims. It is a quite complicated system, how to call this ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When was the entity of Yugoslavia first proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, as a state, was proclaimed by the Serb Prince Regent, Alexander, on 1st December 1918. As a Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes with this name. Not with the name of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were they seeking to achieve by the formation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the formation of Yugoslavia was achieved a political programme based on Yugoslavism. This political programme found its origin in the 16th, 17th Century, particularly in Dalmatia and Croatia, and was developed in Slovenia, in the democratic and socialist movements in Serbia in the 19th Century. The idea was to create a common state of South Slavs from -- including, in some ideal approach, including Bulgarians, and this was already as a project prepared by the political experience of the Illyrian Movement and the Illyrian provinces established by Napolean at the beginning of the 19th century and then supported by several leaders, policy-makers in connection with the ideals, national ideals of 19th century Europe, so the personalities, the Yugoslav personalities who supported this project, for instance, Strossmayer, Raci, Kalas, or Markovic, Polit-Desancic and others were, in several ways, in connection with other opponent policy makers for instance like Mussolini in Italy or Sartoritski from Poland and others that were increasing that idea of nation which was not related with ethnicity. This was typical of the 19th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there a desire to achieve a simulation or was that not the concept, by this process of the creation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have to distinguish the ideal, and then how the situation was implemented. During the First World War and immediately after the First World War, the ideal was shared by a large part of the intellectuals in Croatia and in Slovenia, not only in Serbia. For instance, when Strossmayer created the academy, the academy was called the Yugoslav Academy of Science and Arts in Zagreb and not the Croatian Academy. When the Social Democrat Party in Slovenia was created in the 70s of the 19th Century, this party was not called, "the Social Democrat Slovenian Party", but the, "Yugoslav Social Democrat Party", so this idea was shared by some policy-makers and particularly by Markovic and socialist and democrats in Serbia who had this idea of creating a state, a common state, leaving the form of the language in the first half of the 19th Century, by Ludwig Guj in Croatia and Vuk Stefanovic Karajic in Serbia was an attempt of creating, of establishing the common dialect as the literary language for whole the area of the -- not only for the all Serbo-Croatian-speaking area, they had even the idea that Slovene was only a dialect in this context. This is not a simulation, also, because we have to consider in the context of the mentalities of that time, which is not exactly the mentality of the 20th century, and, you know, many policy-makers, shared the idea that nation was something different from ethnicity. It had a more wide concept, related even with the idea of the Citizen in France. Just to give you an example, when King Alexander thought that Croats, Serbs and Slovenes were three names of the same people, he had the same political approach, the same political culture than a democratic. King Alexander was not democrat. It was an autocratic kingdom, but democratic as Maserik the President of Czechoslovakia was, when he considered also the Czechoslovakian nation existing as a Slovakian nation and not a Czech nation or a Slovak nation with related regions to ethnicity. This was also the approach of Wilson. They had this wide approach and in this sense they considered the possibility of creating Yugoslavia as a state of those, of this common state for all the South Slavs. Bulgarians were excluded only after the second Balkan war, when the Bulgarians attacked the Serbs after having signed an agreement before the first Balkan war. So this was the reason why the Bulgarian was considered missed for the Yugoslav perspectives. This was the aim of those who wanted the creation of Yugoslavia, before the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, if I may ask you, could you slow down just a little because it has to be translated and that is a very difficult job for them, for the translators to do that so if you could speak a little slower I would be grateful. What effect did the World Wars have on Yugoslavia? World War I and II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two wars had different impacts, so we have to consider first World War I, and then World War II. About World War I: This created the conditions for establishing Yugoslavia. It created the conditions for several reasons; the first was that the great modern Empires, the Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires collapsed during this war, albeit many scholars emphasised that both the empires failed in their modernisation before the war started. This is true for both the empires, albeit the Austro-Hungarian empire had only one attempt of take-off and this happened in between 1901 and 1903 while the Ottoman empire had at least two attempts during the 19th century, through the so-called Tanzimat which were supported by the western great powers, particularly. So, anyway, the two empires were unable to modernise themselves to create the conditions for the take-off of the country. The war created the conditions for their collapse. In the meantime, because of this disappointment in their lack of a modernisation process, the wings, who supported Yugoslavism, were threatened because the Yugoslav perspective was envisaged as a better perspective for creating conditions for the modernisation of the countries because of the failure of the modernisation of the great empires. The other reason was a great influence was also, and this must be taken into account, made by the evolution of the idea of nationalism in Europe in the second half of the 19th century. This evolution had a great impact on the policy of the great powers, and this influenced the states in the Balkans. Nationalism which was an ideal of the opponents up to 1860s, 1870s, became after a state ideology. This is very important change. This state ideology was influenced by different elements. First, imperialism. I mean imperialism particularly of the second half of the 20th century. Then the second question was, for instance, the attempts of applying the Darwinian approach to the evolution of the species into international relations, only strong countries can survive in the international context. The third was anti-semitism which was particularly strengthened in France. I can mention the Dreyfuss case and the reaction, the anti-German reaction after the defeat at Sedan in 1870. So all these elements influenced the perception of nationalism, and this was one of the reasons why the Balkan alliance, which prepared the first Balkan war, collapsed, and then a second Balkan war occurred within the former alliance. Bulgaria attacked Serbia and was attacked by Serbia, by Greece, by Romania and Montenegro. So, this is just to show you how these elements were transferred into the policy attitude of the states at the beginning of the 19th century. Then I would like to mention also Italian irredentism. This effect had a great impact particularly on the decision of the Slovene and Croatian policy-makers when they had to establish their negotiation with the Serb representatives on the island of Corfu. Italian irredentism claimed -- heritability is just a term to say that there are unredeemed areas for establishing the national state, and the Italian heritability claimed, not only Trento and Trieste but Dalmatia which was overwhelmingly populated by a Slavic population, Croat and Serb, so they claimed for historical reasons, for demographic reasons, artistic reasons and so on, and this had a great impact in the sense that this created a sense of insecurity with the policy-makers in Croatia and Slovenia, and when they had to establish their negotiation with the Serb representative, they were forced to do the negotiation, to find an agreement as soon as possible, because Italy threatened the possibility of establishing their western borders, that is the Italian eastern borders. So this element, just to remind you, Italy signed an agreement in 1915 with France and Great Britain, before entering the First World War, the so-called Treaty of London, which became public after the Russian revolution when Lenin took over the power in Russia, because Russia had made public, these documents, and in this document, Dalmatia was offered to Italy, but not the city of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, once the collapse of the Hapsburg Empire became a certainty, was there then a conference called in relation to the situation in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the empire was collapsing, it was clear to collapse, Italy summoned, held congress of oppressed peoples in Rome. The congress was organised by the liberals but the government did not want to find any agreement with the Yugoslav delegation, and the Yugoslav delegation, the name was set up particularly by Croats, Serbs of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and Slovenes and the Italian Government did not want to find an agreement with them which increased the sense of uncertainty of these policy-makers. So when the empire collapsed they were, in a way, urged to find any agreement with the Serb Kingdom in order to protect themselves from the aggressive approach of Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, moving on to World War II, what impact did it have on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: World War II was different because World War II arrived when Yugoslavia was already established and when an attempt of modernisation of Yugoslavia, during the kingdom failed, particularly the 1929 economic crisis affected deeply the evolution, the economic values of Yugoslavia, plus it was difficult to find an agreement between the Serb Government in Belgrade and generally the Croats, this is true, but not only the Croats. The Croats in Zagreb and particularly the peasant party, enjoyed the alliance -- this is very interesting -- of the Serb party of the Serbs in Croatia which was against the centralisation attempts of the Belgrade courts of the so-called Carsija and the kingdom. So this was two of the elements of contrast. In addition, we had the influence of when Hitler took over power, we had the influence of the Hitlerian perception of nationalism which added an element of racism to nationalism, and in this sense were created the Ustasha movement after the coup d'etat in 1929 by the King, and this movement was at the beginning supported by Mussolini in Italy. It was armed and financed by Mussolini. Then this movement perceived ideas coming from Italian heritability and from the Hitler nationalism and applied it to the context of Yugoslavia from the Croatian nationalist point of view. So this element clashed when Hitler attacked Yugoslavia in 1941 and Yugoslavia collapsed in a week, in a week this element clashed with the other nationalist approach, this was the Chetnik one, which was supported by the General Draza Mihailovic and was connected to the King, the King who escaped to London, and the idea was in this case to create a greater Serbia or a greater Yugoslavia with a greater Serbia, and Croatia had to be punished, because Croatia was charged to be an ally of Hitler. So, these elements created in a sense two movements, the Chetniks and Ustasha, who clashed with each other, and a civil war erupted immediately. We had the Italian army, occupation army had the first information between April and May 1941, Yugoslavia was attacked at the beginning of April 1941, and I can tell you this for sure because I had the opportunity to see the archives of the Italian army so I had the opportunity to see the notes of the Italian officers sending to the Italian army what was going on particularly in Lika and in the area between Croatia and Bosnia. Thus, for this reason, this condition created the best ground for increasing the role of the Communist Party, led by Tito. This Communist Party was a Yugoslav Communist Party, had a Yugoslav direction with representatives of all the main ethnic groups of Yugoslavia, then Tito had a strategy of war while Dagar Mikaisleovic did not have one, he wanted to wait the arrival of the alliance. At the beginning attempts of finding a compromise between the Chetniks and Tito failed in the fall in 1941 and the two groups started a war, one against the other. Even they -- Tito had more -- wanted to react immediately against the occupation, and of course a support to the invasion of the Soviet Union was also included in this, and this created the best condition. Then Great Britain particularly supported Tito after 1943, when it appeared clear that Tito was fighting against Germany, and the Chetniks, no. However, I have found in the Italian archives the documentation, interesting documentation, by the way, that proved that the Chetnik movements seen in Montenegro already in the summer 1941, but particularly after the end of the year, was financed by the Italian army, by the Italian occupation army, so the Chetniks became more or less allies of Italy until -- up to, until 1943 while the Ustasha became much more close to Hitler and this was provoked by the fact that Italy wanted to obtain control over Dalmatia which was claimed by the Ustasha movement too, and Hitler, anyway, gave to its Italian ally, Dalmatia, so this is one of the reasons why we had this split between the Italian government, Mussolini and the Ustasha immediately after the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened after World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the war in 1945 communism took over the power rapidly. War accounts were settled mercilessly. First General Draza Mihailovic was arrested and executed in 1946. The Albanian revolt in 1944, 1945 was repressed strongly after several months with difficulties for the Yugoslav army. People, 30,000 Croats, general Croats, related to some extent to Ustasha movement, the occupation German army, were all surrounded by the parties or handed back by the British army in Austria and they were executed in the area of Kocevski Rog and Blejburg between Slovenia and Croatia, in this area. The Catholic top, and particularly the Bishop and Cardinal of Zagreb, Stepinac was charged with being involved in supporting the Ustasha regime, to have participated in -- or to have been included in -- to have supported the policy of eliminating opponents, Communist opponents, and the Serb's population in the Jasenovac area. For these reasons he was sentenced, he was not executed. He remained in prison, and died without obtaining his freedom. He was 96, something like this. So this was the reactions against the anti-Communist movements by the Communist movement. Meanwhile, a coalition government was set up at the beginning of 1945 between the Communist Government and those policy-makers who were involved in the London Government and who did not have connections with the Italian/German alliance. This government, this coalition was imposed by Jalta, by Jalta because of the agreement of 1944 between Tito and Churchill. Tito did not implement it, so Churchill requested of Jalta the implementation of this agreement. Tito had to do this, but this alliance was very weak, and it evaporated in a few months, between September and October 1945. So, when the elections were held in November 1945, the campaign was really traversed way of democratic campaign, it was not really a democratic campaign. The opposition made the decision to participate in the ballot only with a box, an empty box, a box without a list, so they did not participate, in fact, with their candidates. But the elections itself were fairly conducted in the sense that a secret vote was guaranteed to the population. Probably we have a map that we can...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Explain the empty box campaign in relation to the document that I now show you. Perhaps the document on the screen can be taken and given to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, looking at that document, Professor, what can you tell us about it in relation to this campaign that you referred to as the "empty box campaign"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the empty box. Box vote is interesting for this reason; you can read down there that the result was, for the Federal Chamber, 88.7 per cent in favour of the Communist Party, which was not in reality, actually, the Communist Party. It was the National Front. The Communist Party was never quoted at that time. This is very important, and for the Chamber of the People, the popular front, the 88.4 per cent. But what is interesting to make a comparison in some of the most crucial areas of the country, of the votes, the empty box votes. You see that for instance in Slovenia more than 15 per cent of people did not want to vote or voted for the least -- the empty list, and then even in Vojvodina, which is part of Serbia, you have more or less near the 50 per cent, the 11.4 per cent of the Serbia, and the 8.5 per cent of Croatia. The figures of Serbia are particularly interesting because if you read, in addition, down, in the notes, Serbia had an abstention of 20.8 per cent, that reduced the fraction of eligible votes for the National Front to 68 per cent, 68.3 per cent, so this is just to give you an idea why I said that the election by itself, they are fair, albeit the campaign was not fair and was not made under the typical democratic rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours as the next Prosecution exhibit. Professor, what was the constitutional model of Tito's Yugoslavia? What was its origins, its source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the constitution in 1946, the first constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The first constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The model was the soviet model, particularly the Stalin constitution of 1936.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was the main features of socialist self-management that you...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Socialist self-management became the ideology of the state from 1950. At the beginning it was a union proposal, and it was applied in some factories around Split and then a law was passed in 1950 and this was the beginning of the self-management system. This system tried to create -- first, the system changed radically between 1950 and 1989 radically. So, at the beginning, this was just an attempt of creating more freedom of decisions in the factories, so only in the factories with a possibility of -- for the working people to participate in the discussion about the production, something like this. This was linked to a lack of planning. This system occurred after the split with Stalin in 1948, so no possibility of planning, because they had no financial sources. They were isolated. It was impossible to create a planning system. For this reason, this system worked up to the end of the 1950s. Then a great crisis occurred, and in 1965, after many, many confrontations within the party, a radical economic reform was passed. This was a very serious and interesting attempt of introducing market rules in a socialist economy. This was the attempt of giving to the factories the right of establishing prices, and prices were established on the basis of typical economic or market economic laws. So this was -- this law was supported by other laws that made possible immigration flows within the country, and outside the country. A passport was given to all the citizens for a period of five years. You have to take into account that a free passport was only given to the population in the other socialist countries after 1988. 1989 in Hungary and for the others even later, so Yugoslavia was the only one country, socialist country that allowed this free-flow of people, under the condition of the dictatorship of the proletariat. This must be all the time clear, but free-flow existed in this sense. Then after the crisis, national and ideological crisis which occurred in the country between 1971 and 1972 the Slovenian ideologist of self-management, Kardelj, made a new reform of the self-management. He created a very complicated system through the constitution of 1974, and the law for the associated labour of 1976, very complicated system based on the structure of co-operatives. If you have an idea, just to give you an idea what was on. This was a system, a general system which permeated the whole of the society. That means not only the factories, but all the activities, agriculture, social services, the law system, the judiciary, the school system, so self-management became the system of organising the society on this basis of the associated labour. But, this created a very articulated society, very articulated society. But, this articulated society had a limitation, a great limitation from the political point of view. This limitation appeared clear with the Djilas case in 1954. Djilas was a very important policy-maker of the Yugoslav communism. He was the Head of the Department of Propaganda, and Education. He was, during the war, he had a very hard line and Stalinist approach towards non-communists, but in the period between 1948 and 1952, 1953, he gradually changed because he had a lot of relations with social democrats party, the British Labour Party so, it changed his idea and he started to write under the approval of Tito, a series of articles where he envisaged the possibility of establishing a kind of dialect within the organisation of the parties. The party changed in 1952 the name from the Communist Party into the League of the Communists. In fact the change was just a formal change but when they started, when they wanted to make this change, they thought that, "league", meant something that, a kind of dialectic should be encouraged within the structures of the party, and for this reason, Djilas started to speak about this, but the orthodox wings of the party opposed strongly. Tito feared the evolution of this thesis, stopped Djilas. Djilas insisted. Djilas was condemned, then he spoke in an interview in the New York Times about the possibility to create -- a bi-party system, social democrats and Communist Party in the social countries. For this reason he was condemned and he became the most known dissident of Yugoslavia. This event made clear to everybody that a great limitation affected the development of self-management and this limitation was the possibility to move from an economic and social ethno-national articulated structure into a political articulated structure because this was an idea originally opposed by the constitution, by the idea that self management was a part of the proletarian dictatorship and because the Djilas event made clear this limitation in the strategy of the league of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the implications of the split between Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The implications --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I will repeat the question. What was the implication of the split between Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many implications. The first implication was that the balance, the east/west balance changed. The confrontation, the Cold War confrontation moved from west to east, from Trieste areas to the Danube River, and both the great superpowers tried to take advantage, in a way, or the United States, in a way, to include Yugoslavia in the western camp, and the Soviet Union tried to withdraw, to get Yugoslavia into the socialist camp. So this changed the relations and both tried to bring their own influence on Yugoslavia. This was the first consequence. The second consequence was that the Yugoslav communism was forced to find an alternative to the soviet system. They had or to accept the western order, and so to change radically their ideological orientation or to find something else, and they did it with the idea of self-management with all the limitations I spoke of earlier. The third consequence was that Yugoslavia, at the beginning, but this can be considered for all the history of the Communist Yugoslavia, tried to lead an international movement. It is less known that Yugoslavia tried to lead an international anti-stalinist movement immediately after 1949, 1950, because the Yugoslav leaders did not understand immediately that the break-up with Stalin was so radical. They tried to find some compromise. Compromise failed, and then... So, they tried to establish their leadership in the sense, with establishing contacts with the socialist party of France, with the Labour Party, supporting some Italian policy-makers who split the Italian Communist Party, particularly Valdo Magnani or Silone and others, given an economic support after the split occurred in 1951. I had the opportunity to see the documentation, so in the archives in Belgrade in Italy, so I am sure about this event, and then, after this, when this attempt failed, they tried to establish a leadership in the regional area through the Balkan pact with Greece and Turkey. They tried to create -- they did not want to join NATO. This was the aim of the United States of America but a clear document of 1952, November 1952, of the party made clear it was a secret discussion with Tito and the policy-makers, where this is conserved, in the archives in Belgrade exclude absolutely this possibility, but they signed the agreement with Greece and Turkey with the aim, particularly shared by Greece to create a new kind of Balkan integration, and in order to attract, if possible, particularly after 1954/1955, Bulgaria and Albania. Then when this attempt failed, because of Greek/Turkish nationalism, confrontation, the Cyprus question, and because of the Stalinisation processes in the Soviet Union, Tito tried to lead the anti-deStalinisation process in the Soviet Union. When these processes failed, after the Hungarian Revolution and the execution of Imre Nagy in Hungary, Tito, who had already connections with the so-called Third World, particularly with Nehru and Nasser started to create a non-aligned movement. So if you compare all these elements you can see the strategy of Yugoslavia to be the leader of an international movement and this was also one of the reasons why the split with Stalin occurred. Then, the last of the consequences of the 1948 split was that Yugoslavia, by inventing, in a way, to a certain extent, self-management, by finding itself in a peculiar position, became a kind, a sort of example for the other countries included in the soviet block from Poland to Bulgaria. It is very interesting. It is not by chance, for instance, that self-management was a claim shared by the Hungarians during the Hungarian revolution, Czechoslavakia in 1968 and by Solidarnost in 1981. It is true that all these movements did not want to apply the Yugoslav model of self-management to their own situation. No. They wanted to just use the fact that Yugoslavia had an independent position to obtain a similar position in the eastern camp. This was the reason why this example had a peculiar impact in the -- even in the soviet camp, and this was the reason why the Soviet Union tried all the time to reinclude Yugoslavia in its camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to have a recess, so see you back here at ten minutes to twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? At present, there is an academic tradition, that -- well, maybe I should say that in a language other than language -- the first is given and the last is accepted. Now, we accepted the first, and we are going to accept the last in this case. In other words, you might pursue it, sir. I think a little Latin does no harm to the solemnity of our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor Bianchini, moving on now, can you explain to the court what the significant features of the 1974 Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The main features were the following; First, the 1974 Constitution outlined a very decentralised state based on six republics and two autonomous regions. Then the state was based on a collective direction, collective on several levels, and on a collective representation. Political representation, which means that citizens as such did not have any opportunities to be represented in any political and administrative body of the country, but only as expression of a collective. The system, the constitution also outlined in a very complicated and wide sense the social and economic system of the country. These were the main features of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what about the presidency? Was there any special feature in relation to the presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The presidency was a collective presidency of eight members which rotated, who rotated in the sense that they had a specific order. This was the system after the death of Tito. Tito was elected in 1974 as a President-for-Life, so after his death, a collective presidency took over power, and with a specific order they had a presidency and a vice-president. The vice-president became the following President after receiving at least five votes of the eight members of the election, and they rotated every year, so every year they changed the direction, the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the main criticism of the system of representation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two were the criticisms. The first one which seems to me particularly interesting is the criticism included in a book written by Jovan Miric, Sistem I Kriza, published in Zagreb. This book made evident the fact that the representation was collective and the decision was taken only on the basis of the consensus. The six republics and the two autonomous regions had, in fact, a right of veto. So this means that, albeit they had a different number of representatives in the two chambers of the parliament, the republics had a certain number and the autonomous region contained a number of representatives, had only one vote. Each representative had only one vote, so they vote, majority, minority, within their own representatives. But then they expressed only one vote, positive or negative, and only the eight positive vote allowed to make a decision. Otherwise, only one negative vote expressed both by one of the six republics or by one of the two autonomous regions could stop the decision. So, the provocative proposal of Jovan Miric was to send to the Federal parliament only eight persons because it was too expensive to send so many people when the possibility to express their votes was only extremely contained. This was one aspect. The other aspect was the criticism which came from Serbia. This was particularly related to the statehood, nationhood of Serbia. This means that even within the Serb League of Communists there were disappointments and criticism on the fact that the two autonomous regions had too much autonomy in comparison with the republics. So in effect, there was no difference between the republics -- the six republics and two autonomous regions on the decision-making process. So, in this sense, Serbs, a Serb wing within the party insisted that Serbia was, in a way, marginalised or punished by the constitution, and this status was already supported before the Memorandum of the Academy of Science was published, was supported by some political leaders, as for instance Draza Markovic in Serbia. Tito, since he was active politically, strongly opposed against this position, as was his reaction -- the last reaction was in Bugojno three months before he was -- he became sick in 1979, when he reacted very strongly on rumours and protests coming from Serbia on these topics because he defended strongly the balance of the ethnic national relations included in the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the circumstances surrounding the SANU Memorandum that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SANU Memorandum was prepared by a group of scientists of the academy in the years between 1982, 1983, up to 1986. It was published only partially by some magazine in 1986, 1987. It provoked a very great crisis, not only in the country but within the Serb League of Communists, and it was published completely, as far as I know, only in Zagreb by Nase Teme in 1989. The scientists who met together in that period between 1982 and 1986 were particularly scientists on Ancient and Middle Age Arts, on Middle Ages History, Modern History, Literature, Philosophy, mainly, and they shared one specific approach of nationalism which traced back its origins on the German anti-alignment Romanticism of Herder and von Schlozer, two scholars of the period -- leaving the period between the 18th and 19th century. They had great impact on the whole Eastern European history, and the main feature of these two scholars was that national is something that you receive from your parents biologically, so you are a member of this nation as you have the colours of your eyes, or the colours of your hair inherited from your parents. So this is something that you cannot change, which is completely the opposite of the Matcini point of view, for instance. Matcini spoke about nationalism as something that is shared on the basis of a consciousness, so on the basis of the -- and we shared particularly not only -- yes, a language, a culture, but particularly we share a common right, a common law. So in this sense, just to give you an example to understand, if an Italian goes to Argentina he can share the Argentinian nationality and become an Argentinian on the basis of the Matcini approach but he cannot, never, in his life, on the Herder approach, so these persons of the Serb academy shared this cultural mentality and they started to write a document as a collective work where they claimed that Serbs were, in a way, oppressed in Yugoslavia, that their idea of Tito was to create a weak Serbia to have a strong Yugoslavia. Particularly they charged Croatia to marginalise the Serbs which was, in effect, untrue, and even in Bosnia, in Bosnia, they charged more or less the same things, taking into account particularly the situation of Kosovo. They started from this, the tensions in Kosovo and because in Kosovo the Serbs were a minority, but the region has claimed, as the south of the Serb nationality, nationhood, and so for this reason they started from this and they charged Croatia and to a lesser extent Bosnia of the same attempts. So, this was the document and the framework when it was written. What is interesting is the end of the document, the last three pages, where the documents made clear that in the event that Serbia cannot have its own role in Yugoslavia in its own right, this is their argument, on the basis of history, of the previous nationhood they had in the 19th century, on the basis of their demographic weight and so on and so on, they had the right to have an alternative as Croats and Slovenes had, which means the right of cessation from Yugoslavia. So this was the document, the particular characteristic of the SANU document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this the first expression or first perhaps significant expression of an assertion of sovereignty or, alternatively, cessation from the SFRY that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the elements I explained previously, I think that, in the recent period, the first cessation came from Serbia. It was included in the SANU Memorandum. The SANU Memorandum created a strong reaction within the Serb League of Communists. The President of Serbia at the time, Stambolic, defined that the SANU Memorandum, in memorandum Yugoslavia, in Latin words, which means a document against the future of Yugoslavia and he opposed strongly this document. He had the support of the local Communist organisation of Belgrade, so in that moment, a split was evident in the Serb League of Communists. When Milosevic, who was the President of the party, started informally to support the SANU document, and first he removed the President of the Belgrade League of Communists, and then some months later he managed to remove even Stambolic. This was the first step in the ideological homogenisation of the Serb League of Communists in Serbia. This was the reaction and for this sense -- and I think that this document represented really the first claim of a cessation. This is not something -- it can appear a paradox, that Serbia, in a sense, claimed to, albeit in a not clear way, but claimed a possible cessation from Yugoslavia. If you consider even the position expressed in another country in Soviet Union in 1989, Boris Yeltsin claimed the same for Russia. He claimed that Russia had the right to secede from Soviet Union. So, it was a discontent that started in the main republic, in the main ethnic group of these two Federations: Serbia for Yugoslavia and Russia for the Soviet Union. This was one of the elements of the troubles that were coming into the top level, and becoming evident in that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, dealing with the 1974 Constitution just for a moment, what was the distinction between nations and nationalities in that Constitution and what was the effect of the distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very interesting question because on this question many misunderstandings had been occurring, particularly in the face of the Yugoslav collapse. In the basic principle, at the beginning of the Constitution, 1974 Constitution, it was stated clearly that -- it was written, coming from the right -- the rights of the -- may I refer to my notes just to quote exactly the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, might he have permission to refer to his notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first basic principle of the 1974 Constitution clarifies that the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia has been created by: "Peoples of Yugoslavia..." "... starting from their right of self-determination, included the right of cessation..." And then on. "People's", the term was not "nation", but "people's". So, the question is: Who has the right of cessation in the Yugoslav context, because in the commonest terminology, used in the books on the newspapers, Narod, "people's", was the titular people of one of the six republics. While nationalities, "narodnost" was the term used for the minorities, including Albanians from Kosovo and the Hungarians from Vojvodina. This was, in fact, the only relevant difference between the six republics and the two autonomous regions in the decision-making process. So, it was in this context considered in the Communist terminology. The problem is that the Communist terminology, does the term "people" identify it with the titular nation anyway, or with all the people living, these people living in the context of Yugoslavia. This was the question, because if you consider the Serb people, just to give you an example, Serb people was the titular nation of Serbia and that, in this context, Serbia, proper Serbia with the two autonomous regions, already, questionable. But if you consider Serb people as a whole you have people in Bosnia and Serb people in Croatia. The same you can tell for the Croatian people. Croats in Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia and even the Croats in some villages, if you want, in Kosovo or even the City of Subotica which has a Croat tradition in Vojvodina. So, this is the question, the Communist terminology established this interpretation, and no one knew how to obtain the implementation of this right. This is evident. This was in the communist mentality. Lenin: When Lenin wrote his articles on nationalities, particularly in 1916 and then after the Bolshevik revolution, he suggested that this right of cessation is a right, and must be declared, but it is not in the interests of the working class to accomplish it. Why? Because, and this was typical 19th century mentality, they want people to modernise and develop a country large enough to develop an economy. So this was not in the interests. This is why, in all the Communist constitutions you can find the quotation, "the right of cessation", but no one -- a legal procedure to join this right because the right was proclaimed but not recognised, because it was not in the interests of the working class and because the Yugoslav Communist shared, anyway, the Bolshevik legacy, i.e. mentioned the connection between self-determination and the proletarian revolution, these considerations must be taken into account in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will ask you some more questions about this later on in your evidence, but did this whole issue of nationals of one side or another, have an impact upon the interpretation of "peoples" in places like Bosnia, when it came to their treatment and by republics such as Serbia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even earlier. Even earlier. When the European Community, the famous Troika started to go to Yugoslavia after the war already erupted in Slovenia, we had two interpretations on the basis of the constitution, and the European Union was unable to manage this situation because they referred to the constitution. The constitution had the sentence and this sentence was interpreted by Slovene leadership and the Croat leaderships on the basis of the Communist terminology. Titular nation has the right to secede, while the Serb, this is interesting, amazing, the Serb policy-makers, gave another interpretation. That is that all the people is not the commonest interpretation. All people, all Serb people has the right to secede from Yugoslavia, so this means that the Serb people living in Krajina, for instance in the area of Croatia, had the right to secede from Croatia to remain in a Yugoslavia or in a state, in a new state of the Serb people. So, they both used the document, the constitution of 1974 to strengthen their own position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But for different ends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. For different ends? Yes, for different ends, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were some of the factors that led to the disintegration of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention, particularly on three factors. The first one is the economic factor, the second one is a social factor related to the immigration flows, and the third one is the political system and the political representation system. Economy. Immediately after the death of Tito in 1988, but the signs were perceived by Tito and even by Cardell, Cardell died in 1979 in February, so they perceived that something was wrong in the economy during the late 1978 and during 1979 but anyway, the economic crisis erupted immediately after the death of Tito. The crisis was based on a very high level of international debt, which was created by the fact that the republics were not, in a sense, under some central control, in this sense. They had the opportunity to establish economic relations with international apartness without receiving the permission of the Federal bodies. So, for instance, the government was informed about the debt by the international economic institutions rather than from the internal republic information system. So when the head of the government, Milka Planinc had finally the picture on the table, she established, she informed the population about the amount of the debt but she put the state secret on the partition of the republics because she feared possible impact on the inter-republic, inter-region relations. The situation led the government to adopt very strict policies, while it was unable to control the autonomous of the republics and regions. This means that a lot of resources were wasted under the control, or they were even used in a very ineffectual sense. For instance, they built factories where they were not needed, or they spent money for having all the republics in the same factories. In this context, the system, the economic system of the country reacted, in order to protect itself where it was possible. So, the economic units, the organisation of the labour, the municipalities, the regions, the republics, tried to protect their own market, their own activities, economic activities, and since 1984 it was possible to speak about an economic nationalism, which was emerging in Yugoslavia, and this threatened the common market, because the more the crisis became deeper, the more each unit were closing in itself. This was one of the reasons why the self-management system showed itself to be ineffective in the economic situation. The petrol crisis in 1973 was also a negative influence because this was one of the reasons why Yugoslavia started to obtain economic support from abroad and they had an international debt, and then when Reagan took over power in the United States, you know that the value of dollars went up rapidly and this also affected the international debt of Yugoslavia, so all these elements created the conditions for the crisis and the reaction in the country was such as I explained. This is one thing. The second thing was the social development in the country, because the country had, in the 1960s and 1970s, really a great transformation, and this transformation was followed by migration flows, or within the country or outside the country, sometimes as a definitive and without coming back migration, or sometimes just temporary migration. For instance, in Europe, when the migration was temporary, generally. This migration, particularly the immigration within the country, were not only from the south to the north, so as for instance the Muslims often from Bosnia or the Albanians went to work in Slovenia or along the Dalmatian coast and so on, not only this, but from the villages to the cities, and they arrived in the suburbs. When they arrived in the suburbs, the social strata were, in a sense, being promoted by the economic development of the 1960s and the 1970s but these structures were, at the same time, the most affected by the economic crisis of the 1980s, so disappointment increased particularly in these structures, in the suburbs of the main cities, or in the village where even the possibility of agriculture offered a possibility to soften the impact of the crisis. The third reason was a political reason. That is the system of representation. As I told you before, the political representation was based on a collective system. This was in principle not only ethnical principle. The representation was deferred, and this is true, that it was a very complicated system, with three chambers in the municipalities, and three chambers in the republics and regions and two chambers on the Federal level, and each Chamber of these had a peculiar representative. The representative of the quarters, the zones in the municipalities, as the local organisations, territorial organisation, or the representative of the municipalities at the republic level, or you had a representative of the labour, associated labour from the factories, or even from the allowed political institutions which were the league of Communists, the unions, the popular front which included the Communist and the independence, the youth organisation, female organisation, Red Cross and so on and so on and so on. So, this was the representation in the republics and regions and, as you can see, the citizen, by himself was never represented, but only as a collectivity or because he/she was politically involved in an organisation, or because he/she was a member of a municipality, of a territory, or because he/she was a worker, but not because he/she was a citizen. This is very important. On the Federal level, the representation was, and even in the republics, based not only on this element but on the ethnic issue so that issue was crucial also in choosing, in selecting the state elite, and the party elite. I have a table on Kosovo, for instance, just to give you an example, what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look at the table now. Might that be given the next number in order, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you see in this table, you can see this table, the sources of these tables are different. I make comparisons with different studies of my colleagues. As you can see, in the notes, it is related to the situation in 1981 which means on the census of 1981 and you can see, for instance, in Kosovo that the Albanians represented in 1981 77.5 per cent of the population, and the Albanian members of the League of Communists were 62.8 per cent of the members of the Communist League, and in the elite they represented a 65 per cent of the party elite and a 70.5 per cent of the regional elite. So, you can see also the Serbs, were this 13 per cent of the population and the 25 per cent of the members of the party, they shared the 20 per cent of the party elite, and the 18 per cent of the state elite, and the others, it is the same for there. So, as you can see, to a large extent, the ethnic ratio was used in order to select the elite of the party and of the state, and this was reflected by the representatives of the six republics and the two autonomous regions in the Federal Parliament, in the two chambers of the Federal Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what effect did that have on...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This had a great impact when the economic crisis arose, because every republic, every region, tried to defend, to protect its own area. So, they tried to protect one collective right, which was not, in a way, contained moderated, by the rights of the citizens, but only by the collective right, so each collective right reacted, protecting itself. The consequences of that was that this system, which was basically in a kind of feudalisation of the whole institutions, if one Serb became the President of one institution, so the Croat had to be in another position, the Muslim in another one. This was, for instance, when they had to select the members of the Federal government, whether the head of the government, the premier was a Croat, the minister of the interior had to be of this republic, and the other of the other republic and so on. So every task was controlled directly by this compromise within the republics and autonomous regions. This was even more strengthened by the crisis and by the ideological approach of communism. Why? Because communism said that no political free-flow of ideas was possible because of the dictatorship of the proletariat, so the obviously possible dialect particulars was the national dialect particulars within regions and republics and this created this context. So, in a context of crisis when you had, in the end, the collapse of communism, you had the collapse of ideology. When you had the collapse of the economic system, you had the collapse of self-management. What remained? Ethnicity nation. This system of sharing the power. This was one of the reasons why the protection on the national ethnic basis was strengthened by the economic crisis generally in the whole of the former Yugoslavia and then with different approaches to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit, if your Honour pleases. What was the first major challenge to the constitution of Tito's Yugoslavia after his death? You have mentioned the SANU Memorandum. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first challenge, significant, we can get even the tensions in Kosovo in 1981, but the first significant relevant challenge against the constitution was the SANU document for the reasons I explained previously. It is interesting that a few months after his death, the SANU challenge in Slovenia, journal Nova Revija published a series of articles under the title, "Contribution for a Slovene National Programme". The document was a little bit different from the memorandum of SANU because it was just a series of articles by different authors, while the memorandum tried to be a document, signed by different persons. However, it was a second challenge. The challenge was by a group of intellectuals towards the Slovene leadership on the basis of the national programme. So, in this sense, we had, for the first time after the death of Tito, two challenges in two republics in -- towards the political -- the Communist policy, and the two leaderships in Serbia and Croatia -- and Slovenia had to react, and they did it, and they reacted in such a way that they tried to follow and to strengthen at least partially these national claims from these intellectuals. So, in this sense, the Kucan and the Milosevic positions became based on the reaction of these challenges coming from a group of intellectuals considering that part of these claims were made part of the programme of the two local Communist organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened in Serbia in March of 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in March of 1989 the constitution was amended, and the autonomy of the two regions, Kosovo and Vojvodina, was significantly contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And who was the prime mover in achieving these amendments, primarily responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue was claimed by Milosevic strongly. It is true that this decision was impossible to be taken without the agreement of the other six republics and for this reason, a very strong clash occurred in late 1988 between Milosevic and Stipe Suvar which was at that time the President of the League of the Communists. In the end the republics accepted, probably because they thought that in such a way Milosevic will soften other pressures in future, which was not the case, because Milosevic had a very important speech in June 1989 in Kosovo when he celebrated the 600 years of the battle of Kosovo against the Turks, which is part of the national mythology, not only of the Serbs but generally in the Balkans, but it was particularly used and manipulated by Serb nationalism. He was very aggressive, and he did not exclude the possibility of armed conflict in Yugoslavia in the future, which created a great concern all over the country.
