It is also true that he tried with, informally, the support of other political persons to overthrow the direction in Vojvodina and in Montenegro between 1988 and 1989, but particularly in 1989 through Solovic who was a person particularly active within the Serb movement in Kosovo, Solovic tried to organise a demonstration in Ljubljana in order to explain to the Slovones why they were unable to understand the reasons of Serbs -- of Serbia in order to contain autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina. Because similar demonstrations overthrown the governments in Montenegro and Vojvodina between 1988 and 1989. The Slovone government made a decision not to allow this demonstration. By reaction, Milosevic ordered the Serb enterprises to cut off economic relations with the Slovone enterprises which is the first real attempt and threat to the Yugoslav integration. The first step towards the disintegration of the country, and this was made by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, did the events of Kosovo have influences in other parts of Yugoslavia? You have mentioned in particular one instance. Did it have any impact in other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh yes, yes. They had great impact since 1981, if we stay in the recent period, of course, particularly because on the Albanian request to become a republic, this was today, the claim in 1981, to become a republic and not a region, in order to have the possibility to base possible -- this was the concern of the Serbs, possible request of cessation on the basis of the Communist interpretation of the term, "titular people", that is now on the constitution. This was the reason why they wanted to become a republic instead, rather than a region. But this was one of the elements that allowed the Serb nationalism to strengthen its position, but this affected also relations within the republics, particularly because Slovene leadership, in several occasions, supported the Albanian claims against the reactions. First, they tried to support Albanians economically. The problem was -- and this was a decision made by all the whole Communist League, but the economic possibilities of Yugoslavia during the 1980s were very limited, so this was not possible, and then with Kucan they supported -- so this was one of the reasons why the Serbs charged the Albanians to support the Albanians, to charge the Slovenes to support the Albanians and this was one of the reasons why the Serbs insisted they were disappointed of the common South Slav state. Let me say, also in addition, that all of these questions have to be considered in the framework of the traditional, for the Yugoslavia, attention between centralisation and decentralisation forces which were represented on the one side, I mean, the decentralisation forces, by Slovone, Croat leaderships and Vojvodina. While traditionally the centralising forces were supported by the undeveloped areas; Bosnia, Montenegro, Kosovo, and Macedonia. The reason was because they wanted a centralisation of the resources in order to receive, then arrange support for their economy. Serbia was in between. Independent on the leaderships, so sometimes supported the centralisation in order to receive the economic support, not only for Kosovo but also for the south of the Serbia, but sometimes not. This was, and this is very important, to be stressed, this was not the case in the period between 1966 and 1972 when Marko Nikezic and Latinka Perovic were the most significant leaders in Serbia. I think they were so open and so clever that probably they must be considered the more democratic and open Serb leadership in the last 200 years, and because they were forced to resign in 1972, this was a real tragedy, not only for Serbia, but for the whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, in the midst of all this turmoil, was there then held elections in the republics in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the Bosnian election? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there elections held in 1990 and where were they held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1990, in January 1990 the League of Communists collapsed, collapsed on the basis of its own national, ethno-national representative or... so that Slovene representative abandoned the party immediately followed by the Croat, Macedonian and by all the others. So, the party disappeared, they separated, and in this context, a series of multi-party elections were organised in the republics. It was the regular, normal order to have election in the republics first, and then on the Federal level. So, in Slovenia, elections were held first in April, then in Croatia, and then during the year in November in Bosnia, and Macedonia and then in the end in Serbia and Montenegro. So during the 1990s, multi-party elections were held all over the six republics of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to Bosnia Herzegovina, would you look at the document I now show you, and by reference to this document can you explain to us the results of the elections in 1990 and perhaps that might be given the next exhibit number. I tender the last Exhibit 23. If I have not already tendered that, your Honours. I think that is Exhibit 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, referring to that document -- there appears a series of initials there in reference to each of the parties. We are familiar with most of them but just to assist, and for the purposes of the record, can you tell us what the initials represent on the chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the figure of the results, the final results of the elections, considering each party. The SDR was the Muslim party, the SDS was led by -- sorry, led by Izetbegovic. The SDS was the party led by Radovan Karadzic and HDZ, the party led by Stjepan Kljuic. Then SK SDP was the party -- and these three parties, as you can see, shared the best results. They shared particularly a result in their own ethno-national basis, so as there was particularly voted by the Muslim population, SDS by Serb population and HDZ by Croat population while the other parties shared the remains. SK SDP was the wing, the democratic wing of the Communist Party. Generally the orthodox representative of the parties became a member of the administration and of the body, of the previous three parties, so they enter, the support the SDR, SDS, HDZ when the party split, and only the most open wings remained in the SK SDP, or in this -- the other party, SJ, as you can see here, this was the party created by the premier, Adno Markovic, the Federal premier, Ante Markovic who had a disaster in Bosnia, according to the polls before the elections, he was considered the possible winner of the elections, but the result has showed completely another perspective. MBO was a party, a Muslim party led by a group of persons, Adil Zufilkarpasic, in the beginning Izetbegovic and then they split, and the others were alliances with the main parties. So the most significant element is that the three parties, the three first parties which tried to represent the interest of their ethnic group of reference, as I can say, obtained a great majority, but they were forced, because of these results, as you can see, or to govern together, or to lead immediately the country to a war, because only one excluded would be -- would -- arose discontent and dissatisfaction in the country, and created condition for a clash. So they were forced to stay together, and this was what happened. For instance, it was very interesting. They divided in a former Communist system, all their tasks. The presidency, for instance, of Bosnia, which was set up by seven persons, was -- and three representatives from SDR, two each from SDS and HDZ. The President of the parliament was a Serb Krasnik and a premier was a Croat, Pelivan. The same also for the ministers. The Minister of the Interior was a Muslim, the Minister of Defence a Croat, the Minister of the Information was a Serb. So, they had to manage the situation in order to save peace. We are in November and December 1990. Yugoslavia still exists, the other events added to a core, before the collapse was achieved, so they were forced to stay together and they had to share the power in this way, and this was the result of the elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened in, for example, Serbia and Montenegro as a result of the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paradoxically, nothing, in the sense that in Serbia and Montenegro, the previous Communist leadership were confirmed by the ballot. Milosevic obtained an overwhelmingly majority in seats because of the majoritarian system of elections. In Serbia, and the same was for Bulatovic in Montenegro. So they, in a sense, they were both legitimated by the vote in their nationalist options, as were legitimated by the multiparty vote, the leaderships in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I tender that document as the next exhibit for your Honours, please. What was the Jovic proposal, and how did it come about and how was it received, especially in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Jovic proposal was submitted to the other members of the presidency of the Federal presidency in October 1990, after the submission of the Croat/Slovone proposal of a confederation. Anyway, shortly the proposal of Jovic envisaged the recognition of recognised international rights and freedom in the constitution. It envisaged a Federal state of six units with a common market, a common national bank, and a government with two chambers, a Federal Chamber and a Chamber of Republics in the Chamber of Republics. The representatives had to be equal for all the republics of Yugoslavia, while for the Federal Chamber he offered two or three options, that it was possible to accept the proportional approach which was supported particularly by Serbia, or to have just a joint -- each republic the same number of seats, or a mixture of the two. So, the proposal of Jovic was a proposal with several possibilities -- several options to be discussed. However the proposal was rejected by the Slovene and Croatian leaderships and the proposal was not discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What brought it about? What caused it? What caused the proposal to be made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What caused the Confederative proposal of Slovenia and Croatia? This was a different proposal. They envisaged a Yugoslavia as a confederation of sovereign and independent states which could have a consultative parliament, a consultative parliament, and a government with one representative of each republics only, and the obligation for the Federation not to interfere in the internal affairs of the republics, so this was a kind of state which does not exist in -- at the moment in the international order, and it was just a -- and they envisaged only a common system, a security system. This was also possible. They envisaged the possibility to establish a common security system. That is all. The proposal was rejected by the Serb leaderships and the proposal was not discussed at all as the others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, who was Jovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Jovic was a Serb member of the Federal presidency. He was a person strongly close to Milosevic. He was strongly supported by Milosevic and at that moment he shared completely the Milosevic political conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, during this period, what was the position of the Federal authorities in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Interesting question. We have to consider two institutions, the Federal Presidency, and the Federal Government. The Federal Presidency was in fact in a great confusion and blocked. This was because in May 1990, 15th May 1990, the Slovone presidency came to an end, it was Drnovesek, the current Slovone premier, and the turn was the Serb turn so this was Jovic who became the President of the presidency. Jovic, during his presidency, supported all the claims, the Milosevic positions, and had a great responsibility, rejecting all the position coming from Croatia and Slovenia, great responsibility in increasing radically the inter-republic tensions, confrontations in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I just stop you for one moment? I am sorry to interrupt you, but you say that the presidency came to an end in May 1990, according to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovic presidency began, and this ended in 15th May 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1991. When the Croat term came, and this is -- and Stjepan Mesic, in this case appointed by the Croat Sabor and the government, had to take over the duty, but Jovic strongly opposed his election, and he voted against. This was the first time that it happened, something in the Federal presidency. Jovic was supported by the representatives of Kosovo and Vojvodina because after the containment of the autonomy of the two regions in 1989, Milosevic was able to control their representative in the Federal bodies, so he had three votes. He managed three votes instead of eight. The fourth vote was of the Montenegro but Montenegro, because albeit it was close to Molosevic, did not take part in the vote. He had other claims, and so Montenegro representative was not in the meeting when they had to vote. So Mesic had the support of Slovenia, a Slovene representative of Bosnian representative of Macedonian representative and his vote, which is four, and to be elected he needed five. For this reason, after May 15th, 1991, Yugoslavia remained without a President of the presidency which created chaos in the country, particularly because the army, the JNA, lacked a supreme command because for the constitution, he was the President of the presidency who has the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned the presidency --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the presidency. The government. The Federal government. The story of the Federal government is quite different. The government was led by Ante Markovic, a Croat a man who had a good knowledge of economic and entrepreneurial aspects and immediately he started with economic reforms. The reform was started on January 1st 1990, and had an astonishingly good result in the first six months. The inflation was completely destroyed, inflation was -- before 1990, around 2,000, 3,000 per cent and it became under 0 in a few months, and he started -- he made the currency, the Dinar solid because he linked the value of the Dinar to the Deutschmark, so he made a series of -- and he started to prepare a new set of laws, because after the first measures, just to block the disaster, he had to accomplish a serious set of laws, physical laws, economic laws, the laws for privatisation, as requested by the International Community. At the same time he tried to go to have the Federal multi-party elections and he tried to dissolve the Federal assembly and to go to the elections. However, this claim was opposed for different reasons, but jointly, by the Serb, Slovone and Croat leaderships. For these leaderships it was much more important to have a not legitimised Federal assembly, in order to have a confrontation with the government, which is interesting, let me say, that the international community never imposed or claimed multi-party elections for the Federal assembly for Yugoslavia while Yugoslavia was the recognised state in the international framework. So I can say that Yugoslavia was the only Communist country which was not -- well, which was not imposed by the international community, multiparty elections. As you can very well understand, through international -- multiparty, and international controlled elections you had the possibility to have the discussion for the future of Yugoslavia in the Federal bodies, and in that Federal bodies it was possible to discuss the future of the country, to dissolve it, to transform it in another Federation, confederation or something else. This was made impossible by this lack of request, and because the three main leaderships, Serbia, Slovenia and Croatia, opposed. In this context, when Ante Markovic tried to implement the new set of laws as I mentioned before, he was opposed by the three leaderships. Sometimes they agreed together, sometimes they formed strange alliances, so, for instance, Croatia and Serbia did not apply the laws or the laws approved by the government, albeit the constitution, the Yugoslav Constitution, and I want to stress that at that time, Yugoslavia still existed, and was a recognised international state, the Constitution made clear that the constitutions and the laws of the republics had not to be in contrast with the Federal Constitution. They were not implemented, or, for instance, Serbia and Slovenia rejected the Ante Markovic proposal to change immediately the 70 per cent of the Federal constitutions, in particular in the parts related to the economic issues, because this would allow the two to start with the economic reforms, and to create the condition for westernised Yugoslavia, and secondly in the parts related to the role of the party, because the party was operating and it was possible to change because everybody could agree on these two topics, and he was stopped by Slovenian and Serb leaderships. Then in the end of 1990 Milosevic, who had a great social situation in the country, and was affected by the risk of social turmoil, made the decision to order to the Serb bank, popular bank, to print money without the control of the Federal Bank which affected enormously all the whole economic proposal of Markovic. Meanwhile Markovic was already isolated in the country because his party created in August 1990, was defeated in Bosnia, and he had a significant support, only Macedonia. So, he was weak, and he became weaker and weaker in the first half of 1994, 1991, when he tried to submit a proposal for a Union of Independent States which was more a proposal of principles, than a real proposal of transforming Yugoslavia, it was gist a series of principles on the basis of, "we just started to find a compromise", but this proposal was rejected. It was arrived in the beginning of June, and on 27th June the war erupted, so it was the end for -- so it was particularly boycotted in this activity and it was not supported by the international community, particularly in one aspect, which is very important for the international community point of view. The multi-party elections of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it was a few days after the proposals of Markovic being rejected that the war erupted. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only the Markovic, it was another proposal, even another proposal. There was another proposal submitted by Izetbegovic and Kiro Gligorov a few days later and this was another attempt at mediation, but according to Gligorov himself, who I know personally, and I met in his cabinet as a President of Macedonia, he told me that the proposal was not discussed at all, not considered at all, and because it was clearly too late -- it was interesting that from January 1991 to June 1991, we had a series of meetings of the six presidents. They met in different Tito villas. They move from one villa to another to find a compromise which was not included in the legal system of the existing country. They tried to find a solution and it was impossible because the position particularly of Serbia on one side and Slovenia, backed by Croatia on the other side, were clashing, and it was impossible to find, in this context, within these six people, a compromise. So, this is also interesting to stress that no one of the President of Yugoslavia claimed the participation of Albanian representatives in this context. No one, included Slovenia, when you asked me before about the Slovenia, actually, this changes according to the situation. They support and not support Albanians suspended, or, for instance, never Ante Markovic was involved in this discussion, so the premier was not involved. This was a discussion within these six presidents only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this process of disintegration, what happened in Slovenia on 23rd December 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Slovenia a referendum was held in December 1990. the referendum was addressed, a question, to the population, whether they accepted the idea of a free and independent Slovenia in the event that the confederation proposal submitted by Slovenia would not be accepted by the other Yugoslav countries within six months. Within six months. This movement of the voters of the referendums were 93.5 per cent, if I remember well, and the support, the option for the possible independence was 88.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So 93.5 per cent of eligible voters participated of which 88.5 per cent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- decided for independent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just add this; this was very interesting. When the six months were expiring in May 1991, Ante Markovic visited Ljubljana and the Ljubljana government asked him to provide immediately in three weeks the budget division, the economic and patrimonial situation of Yugoslavia in three weeks in order to start the proceeding of dividing the debts and the properties of Yugoslavia. This happened in May 1991 and they gave to the government only three weeks to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice the time, and, as I had anticipated, I have not completed my examination-in-chief. I have had discussions with Professor Bianchini, and he would be available on the 26th and 27th of March which is the last two days of our March session, the end of March session. It is my submission, your Honours, that that would be a good time to complete Professor Bianchini's evidence, and I might just say that it is our expectation, at least we are striving to achieve this, that the 27th would be the last day, will be the last day of the Prosecution case. That is our expectation. Whether we are able to achieve that or not, I can inform your Honours better of that at the end of next week, but if Professor Bianchini can be excused now and come back on the 26th, we will complete his evidence in those two days and hopefully at the same time, complete the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. We can go along with that. I think we can also agree that we have reached 1.15 pm. So, we are going to leave it at that for today. We will be back next week, so the Professor will be back on the basis outlined by Mr. Niemann. So thank you very much.
